headline: North Rip Gone Quiet by Day, Loud After Dark — And the Current's Building for Bonito
subhead: Bass have slid off the daylight bite and into the dark, bluefish are still hammering bunker on the rips, and the first false albacore window is closing fast.
body_markdown:
I felt it before I saw it — Tuesday night, running the Southwest Ledge around ten, the water had that heavier, slicker feel under the hull, the kind of surface tension you get when the current's really loading up against the moon. We're pushing toward full moon in early August, and you can already feel the tide building a day ahead of schedule. That's the kind of signal that matters more out here than any number on a screen.

Striped bass have gone almost entirely nocturnal on us, and that's been the story for two weeks now, not just this one. Daytime surface temps sitting in the low-to-mid 70s have pushed the fish down onto structure — the edges of the Ledge, the drop-offs along the North Rip, anywhere there's a thermocline to hide under. I've been marking fish stacked 35 to 50 feet down on the meter in the middle of the afternoon, completely uninterested in anything, and then watching that same water come alive two hours after sunset. The pattern's been consistent enough that I'll say what I said last week and stand by it — as long as this warm, stable weather holds, the bass are going to keep playing this game. Eels drifted on the down-current side of the Ledge after dark have been the most dependable producer, fished on a fish-finder rig with just enough weight to hold bottom in that current, usually 3 to 5 ounces depending on the stage of the tide. Bunker chunks fished the same way off the North Rip have worked too, especially on the last two hours of the incoming when bait gets pinned against that structure. I pulled a 34-pounder off the Ledge Sunday night on an eel, and a buddy fishing bunker chunks off the Rip iced a 40 the same night — both after 11 PM, both on slack-to-building current. Daytime trolling with umbrella rigs and tube-and-worm out past the Ledge has still produced the occasional fish, but it's a fraction of what you'll get after dark right now.

Bluefish have been the daylight show, and a good one. Bunker schools are still thick around the island — you can see them from a half mile off when the birds start working — and the blues have been pinning them against the rips on both the north and south ends. Southwest Ledge in the morning has been holding some real gorilla blues, 8 to 12 pounds, busting bait on the surface enough that you can run and gun with poppers or big soft plastics and connect quickly. I've had good luck with 3-ounce metal — Hopkins and Kastmasters — cast right into the boil and retrieved fast. This bunker-driven blitz pattern has been building for weeks now and it isn't slowing down; if anything it's spreading, and I wouldn't be surprised to hear it's still pushing hard into the bays to our west and north over the next few days.

Fluke have softened up some in the shallower stuff, which tracks with what's happening everywhere south of us — the flat, sun-warmed water isn't holding fish like it did in June. But the deeper structure has kept producing. The channel edges outside the Great Salt Pond entrance, and the deeper water off the southeast corner of the island, have both been giving up keeper fluke in the 20 to 40 foot range on white Gulp Swimming Mullets tipped with squid strips, dragged slow on 3/4-ounce bucktails. Nothing to write home about in terms of numbers, but quality fish mixed in — a few over 5 pounds this past week.

Now the one everybody's asking me about at the dock: bonito and albies. I'll be straight with you — nothing confirmed yet out here. Water's crossed the threshold where we'd expect to see the first fish, and the current is building the way it needs to with this moon cycle, which is exactly the setup that usually triggers it. But building current alone doesn't put fish in the boat — you need the bait to actually get pinned and worked, and I haven't seen that happen yet around the rips or off the Ledge. If I had to bet, I'd say we're closer than we were a week ago, and the next stretch of building tide into the full moon is the window I'd watch hardest. If you're itching to be the first one to connect, I'd be working the rip lines at first light with small metal and epoxy jigs, watching for diving terns and any nervous water — that's usually the tip-off before anyone gets a rod bent.

Offshore, the bluefin slot fishery has stayed steady on the grounds south of the island, which is worth a mention if you've got a bigger boat and don't mind the run — that bite hasn't skipped a beat since the trophy closure kicked in July 3rd.

Looking ahead, I don't expect much to change through the weekend unless the wind shifts. Keep the bass game nocturnal, keep working the bunker schools for blues in daylight, and keep one eye on the rips for that first bonito showing — this is the week I'd expect it, if it's coming at all.
